subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Add a feature roadmap

Ten intended features, each written against what the code actually rests on
rather than as a wish list, because the useful part of a roadmap is knowing
which items are assembly and which are new subsystems.

Three findings shape the ordering:

The pm2-style supervisor is already written. vpn/supervisor.ts implements
backoff with jitter, crash-loop detection, restart policies, readiness probes,
health checks, a bounded log ring and orphan reaping -- the whole pm2 core,
built for VPN engines and named as though it were VPN-specific. Local process
monitoring is mostly lifting it out of vpn/ and giving it a UI.

Docker and Kubernetes exec ride TerminalTransport, introduced in 0.8.0. A
container shell is a third implementation of an interface that already has two,
not a new terminal.

"Local shell support with ghostty" cannot mean what it sounds like, and the doc
says so plainly: libghostty-vt contains no PTY -- zero pty/spawn/exec symbols
across its 30 headers, zero PTY functions among its 189 WASM exports -- and the
full renderer only targets NSView. The real opportunity is its snapshot API for
session restore, which xterm.js has no equivalent for. Framing that as "adopt
ghostty" would send someone down a path with no exit.

Two items are held differently from the rest. The Tauri migration is a standing
direction behind a gate -- port one hard subsystem end to end and measure it --
rather than a scheduled task, because started halfway it doubles the maintenance
surface indefinitely, and it would rewrite most of 48k lines of main-process
TypeScript. n8n's blocking question is whether the value is n8n specifically or
if-this-then-that over primitives items 1, 3 and 6 already provide, plus a
licensing question that is not an engineering one.

Also states two dependencies that would otherwise be discovered late: backups
should follow cron or the app grows two schedulers, and alert channels should
follow the credential proxy or it grows two credential stores.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Bound the session close in the sample clients so an unreachable server cannot hold them up (#838)

Closing a sample client window could block for up to ten minutes. A ManagedSession
cannot close while its connection state machine is inside a reconnect attempt:
RequestClose only moves the state to Closing, and the worker finishes the current
backoff delay and the current reconnect attempt before it looks at the state again.
Against a host which accepts the connection but never answers - a server stopped while
its machine stayed up, a firewall which swallows the traffic - that attempt runs to the
endpoint's OperationTimeout, which the sample configurations ship as 600000 ms.

Measured against 2.0.0-preview.2 with the Reference server, its port taken over by a
listener which accepts and never answers, OperationTimeout reduced to 20 s to keep the
run short: the close returned after 10886 ms, exactly the remainder of the attempt.
With the shipped 600 s that is ten minutes, on the UI thread, because
MainForm_FormClosing calls ConnectServerCTRL.Disconnect() synchronously.

The CloseAsync(10000, ct) the controls were calling did not bound anything either:
ManagedSession.CloseAsync(int timeout, bool closeChannel, CancellationToken) ignores
both timeout and closeChannel and always returns Good. Reported upstream as
OPCFoundation/UA-.NETStandard#4364.

So the samples bound the wait themselves and dispose when it expires - disposing is what
cancels the state machine and with it the attempt in flight. The same scenario then takes
2000 ms of bounded wait plus 17 ms of dispose. The sessions are now disposed either way,
which they previously never were.

ClientUtils.CloseAndDisposeAsync carries the bounded close for the shared client
controls, ConnectServerCtrl, ClientForm and SessionTreeCtrl use it, and the test client
bounds its own teardown the same way.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: bounded cold start at scale - ANN retrieval, shard consolidation, and resumable replay for the Lattice vector plane (#1873)

* feat: make shard-split admission aware of the shape of the load

Adaptive split admitted any shard above HotShardOpsPerSecondThreshold. A bulk ingest sustains write rates far above that across the whole key space, so the monitor split, split again, and shattered the three vector trees to roughly 1,100 leaves against a 64-shard baseline. Splitting cannot relieve a uniform workload: every resulting shard is equally hot and the only durable effect is a permanent multiplication of grain activations.

Admission now reasons about the shape of the load as well as its rate, through a pure allocation-free decision core (ShardSplitAdmissionCore, modelled on WalGcTrimCore):

- Skew clause: max/median shard rate must reach HotShardMinSkewRatio (1.5). A uniformly loaded tree sits at ~1.0 and admits nothing; a genuinely skewed workload still splits exactly as before.
- Occupancy clause: a shard must hold at least HotShardMinShardEntries (1024) live entries, probed only for candidates that cleared every cheaper clause.
- Ceiling clause: autonomic growth stops at MaxPhysicalShardsPerTree (256).
- Cooldown now reads an injectable TimeProvider so expiry is testable without wall-clock waits.

HotShardConsolidationSkewRatio (1.15) is the lower edge of a hysteresis dead band on the same statistic, so a consolidation driver and this split trigger have non-overlapping trigger regions; LatticeOptionsValidator rejects an overlapping pair.

Refusals are attributed on orleans.lattice.split.admission.deferred with new uniform_load / low_occupancy / shard_ceiling reason tags.

* fix: recover the leaf replay flush ceiling as deferred work resolves

The resumable-replay incremental flush (#1513) clamped the per-slice checkpoint advance below lowestDeferredOffset, a scalar that was only ever lowered. The first DeleteRange, TxCommit or TxAbort in a partition therefore pinned that partition's ceiling for the whole remainder of the replay, leaving every further advance to the post-pass-2 reconciliation - which only runs when the entire replay fits inside the activation window. A backlog large enough to outrun that window banked nothing, the activation was torn down, and the next one replayed the identical range: the #1513 livelock, reopened for any tree that uses range deletes or atomic multi-key writes.

Track deferred offsets in a resolvable per-partition ledger instead, so the ceiling recovers the moment an offset drains. Pass 1 applies a deferred mutation in place once every other partition has been absorbed (its cross-partition dependencies are all present by then), and pass 2 strikes each drained terminal off the ledger and flushes the recovered ceiling as it goes. Both safety clamps are unchanged: the checkpoint still never passes an undrained deferred offset, nor an unresolved saga prepare.

Closes #1831

* feat: allocation-lean binary leaf-snapshot codec with transparent dual-read

Leaf snapshot blobs were persisted as an object graph through the grain-storage serializer, so under the default JSON serializer every row cost a property-name envelope and every value a base64 string. Decoding one allocated a string, a scratch buffer, and a fresh array per row, which is a material part of cold-start cost on a vector-bearing tree.

LeafSnapshotBlob gains a versioned binary frame alongside the legacy row slot: a magic prefix, length-prefixed rows carrying raw value bytes, a trailing per-row offset table, and an XxHash64 trailer. Encode measures first and allocates exactly the frame; decode streams rows straight into the entry cache with no per-row intermediate.

Adoption is dual-read with lazy rewrite and no migration step. The encoding is sniffed on load, so legacy blobs stay readable indefinitely, and a blob is re-encoded only on its next natural capture. A truncated or corrupt payload of either encoding is rejected before any coverage is recorded, so it presents as no snapshot rather than as a snapshot that under-reports the prefix it claims to cover.

The trailing offset table is the seam a bounded, key-range-scoped partial hydration needs: a row can be sought and decoded by index without walking its predecessors, and CompareKeysUtf8 gives that seek an allocation-free comparison consistent with the ordinal order the cache is sorted by.

LeafSnapshotBinaryEncodingEnabled (default true) pins the write side to the legacy shape when a rollback to a build without dual-read is still possible.

* feat: honest retrieval-path vocabulary and vector-plane readiness for repocontext

Adds a closed, machine-readable retrieval-path descriptor alongside the existing search and context 'mode' field, so a keyword answer is no longer ambiguous between an intended keyword-only deployment and a real vector-plane capability loss. The five values are semantic.exact, semantic.approximate, keyword.no_embedder, keyword.vector_plane_unavailable and keyword.index_degraded. 'mode' keeps its existing values and meaning, so the change is additive.

Adds a vector-plane component to /health/ready driven by what retrieval actually did, with a TimeProvider-driven fault hold-down so readiness cannot flap across a transient fault, a keyword-only arm so a box with no embedder bound is ready at once, and a startup warmup driver so readiness never deadlocks waiting for traffic. Liveness is unchanged. Publishes repocontext.retrieval.ready_seconds and repocontext.retrieval.unavailable.

* feat: make WAL GC cadence responsive to backlog

The WAL garbage collector deferred its first pass by a uniform offset in
[WalGcInterval/2, WalGcInterval) - 30 to 60 minutes at the default hourly
cadence - and then ticked on a fixed clock regardless of log growth. A box
recreated more often than that never trimmed its WAL at all: a restored
deployment volume showed 559,455 data records against 64 trim records, one
per shard, from a single historical pass.

Replace the fixed startup offset with a bounded stagger drawn from
[WalGcStartupDelay/2, WalGcStartupDelay) (30 seconds by default, so a first
pass 15 to 30 seconds after start), capped at the configured interval. The
stagger is kept, not deleted: it still clears the activation window and still
de-correlates a rolling restart.

Give each tree an independent cadence inside [WalGcMinInterval,
WalGcInterval]. A pass that trims at least one entry - the collector's own
observation of backlog above the trim floor - snaps that tree back to the
floor; a pass that trims nothing doubles its interval up to the configured
ceiling. A busy tree is therefore collected promptly, an idle one relaxes and
costs nothing, and neither affects the other's schedule. Setting
WalGcMinInterval to zero restores the fixed-interval tick.

Trim eligibility is unchanged. WalGcTrimCore.IsEntryEligible, the
coverage-gated trim floor, and LatticeWalGc are untouched; this changes only
when a pass runs, never what one may reclaim.

Publish three instruments so the reclamation rigs can measure it:
orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes (tree, outcome=reclaimed|idle|failed),
orleans.lattice.wal.gc.interval (seconds, tree), and
orleans.lattice.wal.gc.backlog_bytes (bytes, tree). Byte accounting is a
provider capability, so the backlog series is a defined branch rather than a
silent skip: the pass counter is emitted unconditionally, which makes its
absence knowably "not measured" rather than "no backlog".

* feat: online shard consolidation, the inverse of an adaptive split

Adaptive shard split is a one-way door: a tree the splitter shattered has no way back, and neither of the two things named 'merge' in this codebase is the missing inverse. TreeMergeGrain bulk-loads one whole tree into another; ShardRootGrain.TraverseForMergeAsync merges a B+ tree node during traversal. Neither reduces a tree's physical shard count.

Adds a first-class core primitive that folds one physical donor shard's virtual slots back onto an adjacent survivor and retires the donor from the routing map, fully online - no shard is taken offline and no tree is quiesced, because consolidation has to be usable on exactly the busy, already-damaged deployments it exists to heal.

The donor side reuses the split's per-shard shadow-write primitive verbatim. The survivor side is new: a survivor is usually the shard the donor was split out of, so it still refuses the very slots it is about to own again. ReclaimSlotsAsync lifts that seal at both the shard and leaf layers immediately before the routing map flips; without it every folded key would be permanently unreachable.

Durability: a fold never deletes donor leaf state and never releases a WAL materialiser pin, so the GC's trim horizon cannot advance and no prefix becomes trimmable that was not trimmable before.

* feat: add Orleans.Lattice.Vector, an allocation-lean approximate nearest-neighbour index

Ships src/lattice.vector and test/lattice.vector, adding both to the solution.

VectorIndex is an in-memory inverted file over dense float vectors. A seeded
k-means pass partitions the corpus into roughly sqrt(n) cells; each cell owns
its members contiguously in its own float block, so probing a cell is a
streaming scan rather than a scattered walk. Query cost is sub-linear: the
measured speedup over exhaustive search grows from about 3x at ten thousand
vectors to about 14x at a million.

Deletes are first class - a removed vector leaves its cell immediately and
cannot resurface. Results are totally ordered by descending score with
ascending key breaking ties, and training samples in key order from an explicit
seed, so the same key/vector set produces identical results regardless of
insertion or deletion order. The steady-state query path allocates nothing.

A chunked, version-stamped snapshot format lets a durable consumer persist the
index in bounded pieces, restore it out of order and idempotently, and page it
in lazily: applying only the centroid chunks is enough to call SelectPartitions
and fetch just the cells a query needs. Recall is measured against brute-force
exact search by a committed harness and published in
test/lattice.vector/MEASUREMENTS.md.

* feat: meter online shard consolidation commits

Adds orleans.lattice.shard.consolidations_committed (Counter<long>, unit {consolidation}, tags tree + shard where shard is the retired donor), fired from TreeShardConsolidationGrain.FinaliseAsync only after the terminal state write succeeds - so an increment always corresponds to a durably committed fold, never an attempt, an abandoned fold, or a storage-failure retry.

This is the exact inverse of orleans.lattice.shard.splits_committed and the signal that distinguishes a tree that is actually healing from one whose physical shard count is still climbing.

Per the epic ruling on the metrics doc gate, the two required catalog rows are added to docs/lattice/metrics.md and docs/lattice.dashboards/metrics-to-panel-map.md - rows only, no prose, no other line of either file touched.

* feat(benchmark): isolated cold-start and scale rig for the RepoContext vector plane

Adds benchmark/coldstart-rig/, a committed, repeatable rig that measures time
to first successful semantic query on a restored copy of real durable state,
and inspects that durable state offline.

Isolation is structural (D11), not careful: its own compose project, volumes,
image tags and host port; no build section anywhere, so no live tag can be
rebuilt or moved; a pristine master volume the running stack cannot bind, and
a per-run clone so every run starts from byte-identical state. A fail-closed
guard runs twice - over the configuration, and over the compose document
Docker actually resolved - and refuses the live project, any live volume, a
live image tag, a live host port, any build section and any writable bind
mount.

Measures per scenario: time to /health/live and /health/ready, time to first
successful query and separately to the first semantic answer, warm latency,
retrieval path, peak CPU and memory, and container log counters. Three restart
scenarios (first boot, graceful stop, SIGKILL). Machine-readable JSON output.

The offline census walks the file-WAL framing and the grain-state database
with the stack down, and validates itself against known-answer figures.

Includes a synthetic scale mode for corpora well beyond current live size, and
69 regression tests covering the guard and the parsers with no Docker and no
wall-clock dependence.

* test: drive the split cooldown with S2's shared VirtualTimeProvider

Replaces the private ManualClock added alongside the split-admission tests with test/lattice/Fakes/VirtualTimeProvider.cs, adopted byte-identically from the integrated S2 commit d2e64997 so this branch compiles standalone and the path merges as a no-op. One virtual clock in the test project, not two.

* fix(lattice): propagate the new WAL GC cadence knobs through LatticeOptionsResolver

Integration glue between S2 (#1832), which added WalGcStartupDelay and
WalGcMinInterval to LatticeOptions, and S3 (#1833), which added the
resolver propagation guard. Neither branch fails alone: S2 branched
before the guard existed. Both knobs now sit beside their pre-existing
sibling WalGcInterval, which the resolver already propagated.

* docs(benchmark): record that the cold-start census baseline is pre-epic

The pinned census figures describe a deployment whose WAL had been trimmed
once, ever. S2 (#1832) deliberately changes that, so a census taken on a
post-S2 volume will legitimately report a higher trim count and DIFFER on that
check. Say so, and give the -SkipExpectations comparison to use instead, so the
measurement working is not mistaken for the rig breaking.

Also record why WAL reclamation is proved from durable state rather than
telemetry: the container exposes no metrics endpoint and is not going to gain
one, because default-on healing (D5) requires the host to pick up every
mechanism with no compose or environment change.

* test: assert vector index allocation differentially rather than absolutely

An absolute 'allocated zero bytes' assertion against the per-thread counter
passes when the fixture runs alone and fails in a larger batch: tiered JIT and
on-stack replacement can land inside the measured window, and whether they do
depends on what the shared test host already compiled, so an unrelated sibling's
tests flip the result.

Each allocation contract now runs its path at two loop sizes after a warm-up and
asserts on the difference, so a one-off runtime cost appears in both figures and
cancels while a genuine per-iteration allocation survives. The insert contract
takes its differential across two reserved indexes, since filling one is not
repeatable in place. Training keeps its ratio-against-retained-size assertion but
switches to the process-wide precise counter, because its assignment pass may run
on the thread pool and a per-thread figure would under-count it.

* fix: complete the consolidation metric's required edits

Three gaps found against the wave-1 integration gotchas, all of which would have failed at integration rather than here:

1. DashboardJsonTests requires a Grafana panel for every live instrument and its IntentionallyUnpaneledInstruments allow-list is empty, so the catalog rows alone were not enough. Adds an Overview panel (id 61) charting the consolidation commit rate. Negative-checked: the gate fails without the panel and passes with it.

2. A new LatticeOptions property needs a validator rule, not just a resolver propagation entry. Rejects ConsolidationDrainBatchSize < 1 and ConsolidationDrainLeavesPerPass < 1 (neither has a meaningful disabled value - 0 leaves per pass would leave a fold sitting in its drain phase forever), and rejects only a NEGATIVE MaxConcurrentShardConsolidations, because 0 is the supported way to switch automated healing off.

3. The drain allocation test read GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread across awaits, which is meaningless once a continuation migrates threads. Switched to GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true). The measurement was already differential rather than absolute.

* test: make the replay allocation probes differential rather than absolute

Ledger_min_unresolved_allocates_nothing_per_record asserted Is.Zero against GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread. That is not a safe assertion in a shared test host: tiered JIT can compile - or on-stack-replace - the measured loop partway through the measured window, and the counter attributes that one-off runtime cost to the loop. Whether it lands inside the window depends on what the host has already compiled, so an unrelated fixture in the same batch could flip the result. It passed in isolation and failed on the integration branch at 24 bytes - one small object, not scaling with the 100k iterations.

Replace every absolute allocation assertion with a differential one via a shared AllocationGrowthBetweenLoopSizes helper: run the loop at N and 2N after a full-size warm-up and assert the growth between them is zero. A constant one-off cost appears in both and cancels; a body allocating k bytes per iteration grows by N*k, which no ambient noise can hide. Per-size setup happens outside the measured window, and the measurement repeats keeping the smallest growth since allocation noise is strictly additive.

The threshold is NOT merely relaxed - that would hide a later regression. Add Allocation_probe_detects_a_deliberately_allocating_loop as a battery test for the harness itself (mirroring the mojibake gate's own self-check), so a probe that could never fail cannot silently approve a regression. The add probe keeps a ratio bound because its amortised buffer growth is non-zero by design, and the replay probe keeps the process-wide counter (it awaits, so continuations migrate threads) but now takes the minimum over repeats.

* test: declare the two repocontext retrieval instruments platform-only

TenantMetricDimensionHygieneTests scans all of src/ and keys off the tenant LABEL rather than the metric name or meter, so it catches the two new retrieval-readiness instruments that the name-based metrics-doc and meter-dashboard gates do not.

Both emit only LatticeTenantLabel.Platform because retrieval readiness is a property of the host process, not of any tenant's data: a box either can serve semantic retrieval or it cannot, so attributing it to a tenant would be meaningless and would add cardinality for no signal. Recorded as the deliberate edit the gate asks for, with the justification inline.

The list keys on the instrument FIELD identifier (as the sibling _callsCounter / _responseCounter / _replacedCounter entries show), so the entries are _readySeconds and _unavailable.

* chore(release): register Orleans.Lattice.Vector in the release plumbing

The new package introduced by S6 (#1836) needs its publish tag glob and
both docs/RELEASING.md table rows, or it silently never ships to NuGet.
PackageReleasePlumbingTests enforces all three.

* feat(lattice): bounded leaf hydration - activation cost independent of snapshot size

Rehydrating a leaf from a binary snapshot no longer decodes the blob. The
frame is attached to the entry cache as a seekable backing store, and entry
ranges are materialised out of it only as reads require them, so a leaf
activation costs what the caller reads rather than what the leaf holds.

The cache reports the whole snapshot's row count, footprint and live-key
count from the moment it attaches, every key-addressed accessor materialises
the block it needs before answering, and every whole-cache walk materialises
the snapshot in full first - so reads, scans, digests and the canonical hash
are identical either way. Coverage is stamped from the loaded blob's offsets
and a capture materialises every row before it writes, so a partially
hydrated leaf can never claim coverage it does not hold.

A per-leaf resident-footprint budget evicts the least recently used hydrated
ranges, and only ranges still byte-identical to the snapshot are eligible: a
range that has taken a write is pinned for the rest of the activation.

Behind LatticeOptions.LeafPartialHydrationEnabled (default true), whose off
position restores the previous full decode exactly.

* test: make the allocation battery test's loop genuinely escape

Allocation_probe_detects_a_deliberately_allocating_loop measured a loop whose body was 'sink += new long[1].Length'. That array never escapes the iteration and the only thing read from it is Length, a compile-time constant for a newly-allocated array of constant size, so .NET 10's tier-1 escape analysis stack-allocates or elides it outright. The deliberately-allocating loop therefore allocated nothing on the heap, the probe truthfully reported zero growth, and the battery test became the very false negative it exists to prevent. Assigning the running sum to a field kept the SUM alive but did nothing to make the ARRAY escape.

This is the same tiering mechanism as the original defect with the sign flipped: round 1 was tier-1 OSR ADDING a one-off allocation inside the measured window, this is tier-1 escape analysis REMOVING the allocation under test. It passed in a small batch for the same reason the original passed there - the method was still at tier-0, which heap-allocates.

Store each allocation into a static object field instead, so the reference outlives the iteration and no optimisation may remove it, and document the escape as load-bearing so a future tidy-up cannot silently disarm the test. The field is read back in an assertion, which both proves the loop ran and keeps it off CS0414.

Also harden the helper: it short-circuited on the first non-positive difference, so one noisy attempt on a loop that DOES allocate would have been reported as allocation-free. It now keeps the minimum across every attempt and clamps at zero.

Verified by reproduction, not just a green run: with the old body restored and DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0 (full optimisation from the first call, where escape analysis is most aggressive) the test fails with the reported 'Expected: greater than 0, But was: 0'; with the escape restored it passes under both default tiering and tiering disabled.

* test(lattice): shared allocation probe harness with its own battery tests

Encodes the three-part allocation-probe rule once instead of re-deriving it
per test: differential rather than absolute, warmed at full size so neither
sample pays a compilation cost the other does not, and sampled repeatedly
keeping the minimum so one noisy sample cannot certify a genuinely
allocating loop as clean. Set-up runs outside the measured window, and the
counter is selectable so an awaiting path uses the process-wide one.

The harness is proved from both sides. Its battery test allocates through a
static field, which is a definite escape at every JIT tier: swapping that for
the non-escaping 'new long[1].Length' form and running under
DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0 reports 'Expected: greater than 0, But was: 0',
because escape analysis removes the allocation outright. A second battery
test proves the harness does not simply always report growth.

The four bounded-hydration probes now run through it.

* feat(lattice.vector): persist the ANN index durably with incremental maintenance and self-healing

Adds DurableVectorIndex, which persists the S6 inverted-file index on a Lattice tree in bounded chunks, maintains it in place as vectors are written and retired, builds it in the background as a resumable caller-driven pump, and rebuilds it rather than trusting it when what was persisted cannot be verified.

* fix(lattice.vector): keep a mid-build flush loadable, keep a lazy open read-only, and drop the per-partition flush closures

Three defects found in review: a partial ingest checkpoint marked its cell clean so a later flush wrote a manifest claiming more vectors than were committed; a lazily loaded index repaired state it does not own by discarding an unverifiable index and sweeping retired mappings; and the flush path allocated a closure pair per partition for work described by four integers.

* feat: automatic over-split healing orchestrator, default-on with a kill switch

Adds a per-tree steady-state observer that consolidates a tree back down when it is measurably over-split, so an existing deployment whose trees were shattered repairs itself with no operator action.

Gates on S4's shared decision core (IsConsolidationSkew AND IsOverSplit, never shard count alone) so the healer and the splitter cannot oscillate, and drives S5's consolidation coordinator through its start/poll/cancel seam. Bounded and polite: at most one fold admitted per sweep, capped by MaxConcurrentShardConsolidations, yielding entirely while the tree's median shard rate is at or above the backpressure threshold.

Closes #1841

* test(lattice.vector): harden the allocation probes to the epic's three-part rule

Full-size warm-up before either sample; the minimum kept across five attempts rather than a single sample; and the battery test's allocation stored into a static field so it provably escapes. Verified by substituting the non-escaping form, which the JIT elides outright so the battery test reports zero - the exact false negative it exists to prevent.

* test: record the failed-first evidence for the healing allocation probes

Documents that the battery test's escape was verified by deliberate failure rather than assumed: substituting the non-escaping 'sink += new long[1].Length' body reproduces S1's exact defect under both DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0 and default tiering, and restoring the static-field store returns it to green.

Also records why MeasureGrowth keeps the minimum without clamping (behaviour-neutral for both assertion directions used here), and why the full-size warm-up is load-bearing twice - it moves tiering costs out of the measured window AND forces tier-1 promotion before measurement, so an elidable allocation is caught in a single-test run rather than only in a large batch.

* fix(test): make consolidation cancellation deterministic about the phase it cancels in

The coordinator's phase timer is due immediately and, at the default ConsolidationDrainLeavesPerPass of 16, a small test tree drains in a single pass - so a fold reached Swap, its point of no return, before the test's next client call could land. CancelAsync then correctly returned false and the test failed. The product was right; the test was racing a timer it did not control.

Fixed by holding the fold pre-Swap structurally rather than hoping: a new ConsolidationSlowPumpClusterFixture drains one donor leaf per pass, so a 240-key tree stays cancellable for tens of seconds. The assertion is then an implication, not a bet - phases only advance while a fold is in flight, so observing it still pre-Swap (or already abandoned) after the request proves it was pre-Swap when CancelAsync decided. A reachability precondition fails loudly with a diagnostic if the scenario was never reached, while the contract itself is asserted unconditionally.

Audited the rest of the fixture for the same assumption. Progress_reports_the_fold_advancing_and_then_completing asserted InProgress immediately after StartAsync, which the pump can falsify by completing the whole fold; it now asserts only fields StartAsync sets and no later phase mutates, plus the terminal state, and mid-flight reporting stays covered by the deterministic unit test. The split-contention test had the same shape - a split can self-complete before the fold attempt lands - and now uses the same observed-state implication. The already-consolidated no-op test is safe because that path never arms the pump.

Verified: both fixtures 16/16, three consecutive repetitions clean, and clean again under 16-core saturating CPU load (run time 24s idle to 1m loaded, so the load was real).

* feat: default every bounded-cold-start mechanism on, with a kill switch each

Turns the epic's mechanisms into a drop-in upgrade. Opt-in healing heals
nothing, because the deployments that most need it are precisely the ones
nobody reconfigures.

Five of the six mechanisms already shipped their defaults on. Exactly one was
dead on arrival: LeafCachePreWarmCount defaulted to 0, so the pre-warm path
built in #1820 did nothing for the box it was built for. It now defaults to 8,
matching the shard root's own pre-warm fan-out width so warm-up issues one
bounded wave of priming calls per shard regardless of shard count.

Three re-examined defaults are deliberately left unchanged, with the rationale
recorded on each constant:

- MaxLeafEntriesBeforeForcedCompaction stays 0. TombstoneCompactionGrain opens
  the compaction trigger metric-tag scope only when it is non-default, so
  arming it cluster-wide would start tagging previously untagged per-leaf
  instruments and break dashboards filtering on the empty trigger label. It
  also walks the whole entry table on every foreground commit, forcing a
  partially hydrated leaf to materialise in full.
- WalGcInterval stays 1 hour. It is now the ceiling of an adaptive band, not a
  fixed tick, so lowering it would only make an idle tree poll more often.
- WalMaxRetainedBytes stays off. It is a capacity quota whose correct value is
  a fraction of the WAL volume, which the library cannot know.

Documents every switch in docs/lattice/configuration.md: what it does, what it
costs, what happens when it is off, and when an operator would turn it off,
behind a new overview section mapping each mechanism to its kill switch. Two
traps are called out explicitly: reverting shape-aware split admission takes
three settings rather than one, because the physical-shard ceiling and the
occupancy floor did not exist before it; and LeafSnapshotBinaryEncodingEnabled
must be set to false before any rollback that crosses the snapshot codec,
because a build without dual-read sees a frame-carrying blob as an empty row
set over a prefix the WAL collector may already have trimmed.

Adds 131 tests: every mechanism armed on a silo configured with no options at
all, one per kill switch proving it restores the prior behaviour exactly, the
repository-context host picking every mechanism up with no compose or
environment change, and an upgrade-shaped suite that produces durable state by
running the real capture path under the previous defaults and then reads it
back on the shipped ones.

Closes #1843

* feat(repocontext): route semantic retrieval through the persisted ANN index

Semantic search and the context bundle are answered from a persisted
approximate nearest-neighbour index instead of re-scanning the whole
repo/{repoId}/vec/ prefix on every cache miss, so query cost stops being
proportional to the corpus and a restart reloads the index rather than
rebuilding it.

Approximate becomes the default and exact remains available by
configuration (LATTICE_REPOCONTEXT_SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL=exact), which keeps
the documented contract truthful rather than silently substituting a
bounded-recall answer under an unchanged mode. Measured recall@10 against
the exact oracle on the same corpus is 1.0000 clustered and 0.8205
unclustered, against published floors of 0.95 and 0.55.

While an index is still building - the state of any deployment that has
not indexed itself yet - the plane declines and the exact scan answers, so
retrieval keeps working with complete recall throughout and never collapses
to keyword. The response reports the weaker approximate claim because the
retrieval-path declaration is per index rather than per query; the build
state is reported out of band, per repository and embedding space, through
transition logs and a progress accessor. A building index is never reported
as a degraded one.

The index is maintained in place from the write seam that already
invalidates the warm candidate cache, so it needs no scan to stay coherent
and can never return a vector the store of record no longer holds.

* fix(repocontext): grant and sweep the approximate index tree on the host

The persisted index sits on a tree of its own, and the container host runs a
default-deny access gate that seeds one Allow rule per tree it knows about.
The index tree was not on that list, so every read and write the index made
would have been denied in the real deployment - invisibly, because the
retrieval plane is deliberately fault-tolerant: the build faults, is caught,
logged and re-armed, retrieval keeps serving correctly through the exact
scan, and the index simply never finishes building. No unit test would have
caught it, because none of them go through the gate.

Repository teardown had the same gap from the other direction: it sweeps
every tree holding a repository's data, so an index left off that list would
outlive its repository and be loaded again by a later repository registered
under the same id.

Both follow from one list serving two different questions. The tree-name map
now separates them: All remains the replication enrolment contract, which
deliberately excludes a wholly derived local tree, and the new LocalDerived
and AllIncludingLocalDerived express "holds this repository's data". Teardown
and the host's grant list use the latter, and the host guard now asserts that
relationship rather than plain equality, so a future local-only tree cannot
be silently left ungranted.

* test(repocontext): wait on the readiness endpoint itself, not one of its components

/health/ready became the conjunction of the lifecycle-phase check and the
new vector-plane retrieval check (S7, #1837), but the host fixture's
WaitForReadyAsync still waited only on RepoContextReadinessState. The
retrieval half is driven asynchronously by RepoContextRetrievalWarmupService
off ApplicationStarted, so the helper returned before the endpoint agreed
and raced the assertion it exists to establish.

Polling the endpoint rather than a component is deliberate: it is what an
orchestrator observes, so the helper cannot silently drift into a weaker
precondition the next time the probe's composition changes.

Found by the coordinator's integration lane, which sub-agents do not run.

* test: wait on the real /health/ready contract in the host integration fixture

/health/ready is now the conjunction of the lifecycle-phase check and the vector-plane retrieval check, but WaitForReadyAsync still waited on the lifecycle half alone. The lifecycle half flips as soon as the access grant is seeded, well before the retrieval warmup has proven the plane can serve, so the helper returned while the endpoint could still answer 503.

Poll the endpoint itself until 200 instead. That is what an orchestrator does, it is the contract the tests actually depend on, and it cannot drift again the next time the composition changes. All four callers now wait on the real signal rather than a weaker one.

Also pin which arm of the readiness machine makes this configuration ready. The host binds an embedding provider unconditionally, so the keyword-only arm cannot fire here; it is the no-repositories-indexed arm that reaches Serving. Asserting it turns a regression that would leave the box permanently 503 into a clear failure rather than a mute timeout.

* test(coldstart-rig): baseline the adoption proof and record three structural findings

Measures a restored copy of the live RepoContext volume on the isolated rig
(#1844), and records what it actually shows rather than what was expected.

Three findings, all reproduced from durable state rather than inferred:

- The vector trees are NOT over-split. Every tree, including all three vector
  trees, sits at exactly 64 physical shards on the PRISTINE pre-epic master as
  well as after the upgrade. The 1,110 / 1,073 / 454 figure the epic is built on
  counts leaf grains; adaptive split and consolidation operate on shards.
- Consequently the healing orchestrators have nothing to fold. All eleven are
  armed with their keepalive reminders and persist NotOverSplit, which is the
  correct decision. Recorded so the absence of folding is not read as a defect.
- The ANN index build never completes on this corpus: it aborts every attempt
  with EnumerationAbortedException out of RepoContextVectorSource.CountAsync and
  retries forever. Retrieval stays correct through the exact scan, so the
  symptom is silent.

Also fixes two latent rig defects found by using it: prepare-master.ps1 crashed
under StrictMode on a staging manifest written by an older revision instead of
re-extracting, and -SkipClone destroyed the working volume it promised to reuse
because the warm-up cloned unconditionally.

Adds -QueryFromLive to run-cohort.ps1, because readiness became the conjunction
of the lifecycle check and vector-plane retrieval readiness, so a cohort that
gates its first query on readiness would report that honesty improvement as a
cold-start regression. Adds -SqliteVolume to inspect-state.ps1, snapshot-volume,
observe-healing and verify-corpus, and the three census queries behind the
findings. Regression suite 66 -> 77 tests.

* fix(repocontext): stop a progress hint aborting the whole ANN index build

Measured on a restored copy of the live deployment (#1844): the approximate
index NEVER completed a build there. Every attempt aborted with
EnumerationAbortedException and retried on the next query, forever, so no index
was ever persisted and query cost stayed proportional to corpus size. Retrieval
stayed correct throughout because the exact scan answers while a build is in
flight, which is exactly what made it silent - the symptom is 'cold start never
improved', with only a warning in the log.

Three independent causes, all on the same path:

- RepoContextVectorSource.CountAsync walked the repository's entire vector
  prefix through the RAW ILattice.KeysAsync stream. That stream is documented to
  surface EnumerationAbortedException when the remote enumerator is reclaimed
  mid-scan and is marked EditorBrowsable(Never) so callers reach for
  ScanKeysAsync instead. Walking the whole prefix activates every leaf of the
  metadata tree, which outlives the enumerator on a real corpus.
- The shared eight-reconnect budget was then also too small, because every abort
  is another cold leaf activation and the tree has far more than eight leaves to
  activate. Raised for this walk only. The budget bounds retries, not work: each
  reopen resumes strictly after the last key seen.
- CatchUpAsync treated a failure to obtain the count as fatal, even though the
  count only decides whether to SKIP the repair. Failing to get it now means
  'repair', which is the safe direction and the one the upper-bound case already
  takes.

Applies the same raw-stream fix to the three sibling call sites of the bug
class: the vector writer's retirement listing (where a short list would orphan
vectors), and the vector index store's own reload scan and prefix delete (where
a short read would fail the reload the persisted index exists to provide).

Tests fail against the previous implementation with the production exception.

* docs: correct the over-split premise that S14's measurement disproved

Measurement on a restored copy of the real deployment found every tree,
including all three the embedder writes, at exactly the base 64 physical
shards. The thousand-plus figure the epic quoted counts leaf grains - B+ tree
nodes inside a shard - not shards, and a leaf count is neither what adaptive
split creates nor what consolidation folds.

So the healing orchestrator's NotOverSplit decision on that deployment is
correct, and consolidation was not what fixed it. Consolidation remains a real
missing capability, since a split was previously a one-way door; the prose now
says that rather than implying the deployment was repaired by it. The observed
cold-start cost was a grain activation per leaf, which bounded hydration and
the approximate index address directly.

* test(coldstart-rig): record the post-fix cohort and invert the contention advice

Full before-and-after set across three runs and three restart scenarios each,
plus the finding that explains why the headline did not move.

TIME TO FIRST SEMANTIC QUERY: NO ATTRIBUTABLE CHANGE. first-boot 87.7s -> 100.6s,
graceful 42.4s -> 57.4s, sigkill 37.2s -> 47.2s. Not one delta exceeds its own
run-to-run spread (26-99%), so under D10 none may be attributed in either
direction, and the point estimates trend worse rather than better. The epic's
'materially reduced' criterion is not met by this measurement. Every sample
answered semantic on both sides, 9 of 9 each.

WARM LATENCY AFTER A FIRST BOOT: A REAL, ATTRIBUTABLE IMPROVEMENT. p50 goes from
15,959/5,307/5,368 ms to 210/298/1,987 ms, ranges completely disjoint, every
sample semantic on both sides. On the two restart scenarios the ranges overlap
and nothing may be attributed.

F-D, THE REASON: with the build fixed, no build fails, but the index only
RELOADED persisted state on one activation out of nine - the other eight opened
NotStarted holding zero vectors. The one that reloaded held 4,096 of ~35,800
vectors after two prior scenarios. The build streams the whole corpus and
persists at flush boundaries, and a scenario lasts two to three minutes, so a
restart almost always arrives before the first flush. The benefit is earned over
tens of minutes of uptime, not at the first restart, and a cohort built out of
short restart cycles cannot show it.

Also records that retrievalPath cannot detect a missing index: it reported
semantic.approximate for 100 minutes while no index existed, which is correct
under S12's floor semantics but means warm latency is the only observable that
separates the two states.

Inverts the rig's contention advice. It previously told the operator to stop
competing containers before attributing a delta, while offering no supported way
to do so; that advice was followed manually against the live deployment during
this work. The guard was never bypassed - Invoke-RigCompose scopes every call to
its own project and runs the guard first, there is no unscoped compose path and
no prune. The gap was the guidance, not the guard, so a contended cohort is now
RECORDED as contended and its spread reported as the host's floor. No quiesce
verb was added: a verb that stops other people's containers should not exist.

* fix(repocontext): let a background index build absorb a transient fault

Second half of the #1844 convergence defect, authorised by the epic coordinator
after the first fix exposed it.

A background build was a SINGLE attempt: any fault tore the build task down,
logged, and set BuildArmed back to zero so the next QUERY started a fresh
attempt. The stated intent - re-arming is 'naturally rate-limited by query
traffic instead of by a timer nobody can see' - is sound for a CHEAP retry and
wrong for an expensive one. A build resumes from its last FLUSHED checkpoint, so
a fault costs every vector ingested since that flush, and the resumed attempt
re-opens the index before making any forward progress.

Measured on a restored copy of the live deployment: a corpus of roughly 35,800
vectors faulted about once per flush boundary with a 30-second Orleans response
timeout against a saturated shard root, so query-gated re-arming turned a
TRANSIENT fault into PERMANENT non-convergence. The index sat at one flush of
4,096 vectors and never reached Ready, so query cost stayed proportional to
corpus size and cold start could not improve. That is a defect against the
stated intent rather than a change of intent.

Two changes:

- RunBuildAsync retries in place with a short, capped, linear backoff and
  resumes from the checkpoint, before falling back to the query-gated re-arm.
- CatchUpAsync takes an explicit probeSource flag instead of always paying the
  O(corpus) shortfall walk. An index this activation streamed itself knows what
  it covers and anything written since arrives through the writer's write-through
  seam; only an index reaching Ready at OPEN, or one resumed part-built, needs
  the probe. That walk is the most timeout-prone call in the build.

Deliberately NOT changed, per the authorisation: the resilient scan wrapper
still surfaces TimeoutException rather than swallowing it (a bounded in-place
retry is the right place to absorb it), and the 30-second response timeout,
shard-root reentrancy and index-tree provisioning are untouched - those are the
follow-up.

Tests fail against the previous implementation: a source scripted to throw
TimeoutException on consecutive attempts leaves the build permanently
Bootstrapping, and the probe is re-paid per attempt.

* test(coldstart-rig): final adoption verdict after both convergence fixes

Completes the #1844 adoption proof and states the verdict at the top rather than
leaving it to be inferred from a table.

VERDICT. The epic does NOT demonstrate its headline goal on a restored copy of
the real volume: time to first semantic query is unchanged within the noise floor
on every scenario, against both a quiet-host and a contended-host baseline, and
no delta in either direction exceeds its own run-to-run spread. It DOES
demonstrate a large attributable win in warm query latency on a freshly restored
box - p50 from 5,307-29,271 ms down to 199-264 ms, ranges nowhere near
overlapping, every sample semantic on both sides. It loses no data. It is a
genuine drop-in with no operator action.

Final cohort compared against the CONTENDED pre-epic baseline, because both ran
with the same two unrelated containers: first-boot 74.2s -> 118.6s (spread
94.8%), graceful 61.4s -> 47.7s (spread 57.8%), sigkill 63.1s -> 33.7s (spread
49.9%). The two restart scenarios now trend the right way and sigkill at -47%
against a 49.9% spread is the closest anything came to clearing the bar, but it
does not clear it and the report does not claim it does. first-boot got slower
because a box that now converges spends CPU converging.

Records the three defects the measurement found that thirteen sub-issues of
tests did not, and why each was invisible to a unit test. Corrects an earlier
draft that reported a 10,016-symbol data loss: that was the fixture comparing a
finished ingest against a freshly cloned mid-ingest master, not the epic, and the
comparator and its method note now prevent the repeat. States plainly what this
rig cannot prove - key-level set equality for structural records, because the
restored volume resumes an index job against a live workspace that has changed -
and that memory, the one population no re-index could reconstruct, held exactly
at 211 entries in every comparison.

Collects everything that did NOT improve in one section, and explains that the
readiness figure moving from 3.7-12.1s to 36-237s is readiness becoming honest
rather than a regression. Defers the synthetic scale run and the long-horizon WAL
and snapshot census, with reasons.

* docs(coldstart-rig): correct the isolation claim about the live image tag

An earlier draft asserted repocontext-mcp:local was unmoved from start to finish.
By the end of the run it had moved, f5d3c01d -> 7a8318c4, and the claim was
stronger than the evidence supported.

It was not this work. The new image also carries candidate-ca54aef0 and the
previous one is still present as rollback-20260901-0206 - the live deployment's
own promote-and-keep-a-rollback ritual, timestamped after its operator restarted
the container. This run wrote exactly three tags: coldstart-rig, s14-preepic and
s14-postepic. The rig's guard lists repocontext-mcp:local as a forbidden
DESTINATION, so the rig could not have written it even by mistake.

Restates the isolation section as what was actually verified.

* docs: stop citing the disproven over-split figure in the consolidation planner

S14's measurement against a restored copy of the real deployment found every tree, including all three the embedder writes, sitting at exactly its base 64 physical shards - never over-split. The 1,110 / 1,073 / 454 figure the epic was built on counted leaf grains (B+ tree nodes inside a shard), which is neither what adaptive split creates nor what consolidation folds.

TryPlanNext's comment asserted that thousand-plus physical-shard reading as observed fact to justify its single-pass counting. The optimisation is still correct and stays - O(slots + shards) beats O(shards x slots) for any tree with many shards - but the justification now stands on the complexity argument alone, and notes that autonomic splitting is bounded by MaxPhysicalShardsPerTree (default 256), so a genuinely high count arrives via an explicit ReshardAsync.

Comment-only; no behavioural change. Planner and coordinator unit tests 100/100, em-dash and mojibake gates green, build clean.

* test(lattice.vector): warm the allocation probes at full size and take repeats

This fixture was cited as the worked example for the epic's allocation-probe
rules, but was missing two of them: it warmed at a small constant (200/100/50)
against much larger measured windows, and took a single sample pair.

Warming below the measured size leaves the method at tier-0 when measurement
starts, so a tier-1-only effect - an elided non-escaping allocation, or an
on-stack-replacement cost landing inside the window - either hides or is
attributed to the loop. That is why one such defect in this epic appeared to
need a particular batch composition to surface: it needed a bigger warm-up, not
luck. A single sample pair likewise lets one noisy window decide the result.

The helper now warms at the larger measured size and repeats five times keeping
the smallest growth, clamped at zero. No call site and no asserted budget
changed. Verified 409/409 under default tiering and under
DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0, three consecutive runs.

* test(lattice.vector): align the S6 allocation fixture with all four probe rules

The canonical worked example was missing two of the four rules: it warmed at fixed constants (200/100/50) against much larger measured windows, and took a single sample with no repeats. It now warms at the full doubled window and keeps the minimum across five attempts, and gains a battery test whose sink escapes into a static field so the JIT cannot elide it. No probe changed what it measures and no budget was adjusted; the training ratio is 1.01x before and after.

* test: stop describing the healing test shapes as a measured production shape

S14 measured the real deployment at exactly its base 64 physical shards on every tree. The 1,110 / 1,073 / 454 figure the epic was founded on counts leaf grains - B+ tree nodes inside a shard - which is neither what adaptive split creates nor what consolidation folds, so no tree was ever observed in the over-split shape these tests describe.

The numbers remain good test data and no assertion changes; they are simply relabelled as hypothetical stress scales rather than observations, and the note records the tell that was missed: a count far above MaxPhysicalShardsPerTree (default 256) cannot be a physical shard count, because the ceiling would have stopped it.

Comment-only except one test rename (A_tree_in_the_measured_damage_shape_converges -> A_tree_in_a_severely_over_split_shape_converges).

* test: relabel the previous-defaults upgrade shape as hypothetical, not measured

The last surviving comment asserting the disproven epic premise. S14 measured the real deployment at exactly its base 64 physical shards on every tree; the 1,110 figure counts leaf grains, not physical shards. Comment-only - no assertion, literal, or test name changed - and the note records the tell that was missed: a count far above MaxPhysicalShardsPerTree (default 256) cannot be a physical shard count, because the ceiling would have stopped it.

* docs: correct the epic changelog headline the measurement disproved

The entry led with 'now starts fast'. The epic's own adoption proof (#1844)
showed time to first semantic query did not improve attributably on a restored
copy of the real deployment - every delta sat inside its own run-to-run spread.
The headline is now 'serves fast once warm', and the entry closes with the
measured outcome: the warm-latency win that is real and attributable, the
cold-start result that is not, and why (the index build does not finish inside
a restart cycle at that corpus size).

Every individual mechanism claim was already accurate - each states a cost model
rather than an end-to-end outcome. It was the headline that generalised past
what was measured. Found by S9 correcting the same overclaim in its own durable
memory and prompting a check of the shipped prose.

* fix: stop root promotion minting a root whose ChildrenAreLeaves bit lies

CompletePromotionAsync guarded its deeper-race branch on the raw
state.State.RootIsLeaf flag. When that flag lies - true over a root that
is actually a BPlusInternalGrain - the guard skips itself, control falls
through to the wrap, and a NEW root is persisted with ChildrenAreLeaves
true over internal children. SeedChildParentAsync then resolves that
child as IBPlusLeafGrain and throws InvalidCastException.

The site both throws and mints the state that causes the next throw, so
one occurrence bakes the condition that makes the next occurrence skip
the guard. A census of a pristine pre-epic production volume found 96 of
841 shard roots already carrying it (vector-metadata 64/64,
vector-membership 32/64, vector-payload 0/64, all other trees 0), so this
predates the epic; the new consolidation chaos fixture is what found it.

Two changes, both at the narrowest seam:

- The deeper-race guard now uses RootIsLeafTyped rather than the raw
  flag, so a lying flag no longer skips it.
- Before the wrap persists childrenAreLeaves, it is forced false when the
  child is not leaf-typed, so no new lying node can be minted even if a
  caller reaches here with a bad flag. IsLeafGrainId returns true under a
  non-runtime factory, so this degrades to the historical behaviour for
  test fakes.

Verified: build 0/0, and the InvalidCastException is entirely gone from
ShardConsolidationChaosTests (0 cast faults, against 21-30 per run
before). The fixture still fails on a separate acknowledged-write-loss
assertion that the cast was masking; that is tracked separately and is
not addressed here.

Refs #1883

* Revert "fix: stop root promotion minting a root whose ChildrenAreLeaves bit lies"

This reverts commit 8331abe8f0258b2c8d282726c2082438636179d1.

* fix: decide root-promotion child level by node type, not the RootIsLeaf flag

ShardRootGrain.CompletePromotionAsync wrapped a new internal root above the
current root and seeded it with childrenAreLeaves computed from persisted
flags. When the persisted RootIsLeaf bit lies (true over an internal root -
the issue-899 inconsistent state, found on 96 of 841 shard roots on a
pristine pre-epic production volume) the deeper-race guard was skipped,
because it too read the raw flag, and the wrap seeded an INTERNAL child as
a leaf. BPlusInternalGrain.SeedChildParentAsync then resolved that child
through IBPlusLeafGrain and threw:

  InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type
  'BPlusInternalGrain' to type 'IBPlusLeafGrain'

That is the fault failing ShardConsolidationChaosTests on the epic branch.
Confirmed by stack trace, not inference: every captured fault originates at
CompletePromotionAsync -> InitializeAsync -> SeedChildParentAsync, reached
from a plain ILattice read/write via PrepareForOperation. No consolidation
frame is involved; consolidation's fixture merely supplies the split
pressure and forced-deactivation cycle that opens the window.

The site does not only THROW the fault, it MINTS it: the wrap persists a new
root whose ChildrenAreLeaves bit lies about its own children, which is
precisely the state that makes the next promotion on that shard skip the
guard again. The condition is therefore self-perpetuating, which explains
how it accumulated on real deployments.

Fix, at the one seam that mints it, using the existing issue-899 primitives:
- PromoteRootAsync and CompletePromotionAsync decide the deeper-race guard
  by RootIsLeafTyped instead of the raw RootIsLeaf flag.
- CompletePromotionAsync clamps childrenAreLeaves to false when the
  surviving root child is not leaf-typed, so a lying flag can never persist
  a new root that misdescribes its children.

Both degrade to today's behaviour when the grain factory cannot resolve the
leaf grain type, as every other issue-899 guard does.

Regression coverage is deterministic and does not depend on a chaos race:
ShardRootGrainPromotionInconsistentRootFlagTests builds a shard root whose
RootIsLeaf flag lies over an internal root id and pins all three legs. Its
harness deliberately makes the leaf-grain-type probe resolvable (via
IGrainBase) so IsLeafGrainId is live - a plain substitute factory silently
no-ops the guard, which is why this defect survived the existing unit
coverage. One leg asserts that liveness so the others cannot pass vacuously.

Audit result for issue 1883: all eleven listed raw RootIsLeaf read sites,
plus two the list missed (ShardRootGrain.cs 2334 and 2403), are already
guarded downstream by DescendToLeafForKeyAsync, DescendToLeafAsync or
DescendToEdgeLeafTypeGuardAsync. The two promotion sites fixed here were not
on that list.

Refs #1883

* fix: remove non-default initializers from persisted leaf/internal flags

The grain-storage serializer omits any member equal to the CLR type default.
Raw blobs read off a pristine pre-epic production volume show it directly -
IsRegistered:true present, IsDeleted (false) absent, RootIsLeaf absent:

  {"RootNodeId":"bplusinternal/6f95...","PendingPromotionRootWasLeaf":true,
   "IsRegistered":true, ...}

A persisted member whose "off" value IS the type default, carrying a
non-default property initializer, is therefore LOSSY IN ONE DIRECTION: a
correctly written false is omitted by the serializer and resurrected as true
by the initializer on load. The writing code is correct and the value is
still destroyed.

This is the origin of issue 899 / issue 1883. It is not a logic defect and
nothing ever minted it: CompletePromotionAsync writes RootIsLeaf = false
correctly, and the round trip inverts it. At runtime every internal-rooted
shard root on the volume - 160 of 160, not the 96 that persist it literally -
presents RootIsLeaf = true over an internal root, which is the
InvalidCastException this branch already contains at the traversal layer.

Exactly two members in the state POCOs have this exact shape, and the second
was unfired rather than absent:

  ShardRootState.RootIsLeaf         confirmed corrupt in production
  InternalNodeState.ChildrenAreLeaves  armed; reads clean only because no
                                       tree has reached depth 3

ChildrenAreLeaves is the more dangerous of the two. Every internal node today
genuinely has leaf children, so true is not the type default, is written, and
survives. The first node to gain INTERNAL children writes false, has it
omitted, and reloads claiming leaf children - blind-casting an internal node
to IBPlusLeafGrain on the read path. The trigger is ordinary tree growth
rather than a fault, so it is certain rather than possible. Fixing only
ShardRootState would have left it armed and unowned.

Fix: delete the initializers so the type default carries the "off" value and
an omitted member reconstructs as exactly what was written.

Safety, established by enumerating every assignment site rather than by
inspection of the declarations:

  RootIsLeaf =         BulkLoad 146(true) 194(false), ShardRootGrain 1633(true)
                       1659(rollback), Traversal 1184(false)
  ChildrenAreLeaves =  BPlusInternalGrain 118, 129(rollback), 155, 166(rollback)

Both are always assigned explicitly, and false is written ONLY when installing
an internal root / internal children. So for both POCOs:

  absent-in-blob  <=>  false was written  <=>  the node really is internal

which makes this a lossless repair rather than a reinterpretation, and it
self-heals every shard whose blob is still clean-but-latent with no migration.
It is also provider-independent: absent reads false under a default-omitting
serializer, present-false reads false under one that writes everything. The
initializer is never load-bearing on a fresh state either - every raw flag
read is guarded by a RootNodeId null check or paired with IsLeafGrainId, and
RootIsLeafTyped is false with a null root regardless.

Coverage is a structural contract over the state POCOs, NOT a round-trip test,
and that choice is deliberate. The hazard belongs to the grain-storage
serializer, not to Orleans' core binary serializer: a round trip of
ShardRootState through Serializer preserves false correctly (verified), and
every cluster fixture here registers AddMemoryGrainStorage, so a cluster
reactivation test would pass whether or not the defect is present. That is
why the existing suite never caught this, and a round-trip test through the
provider this suite configures would be a check that cannot fail.

The contract test also surfaced two further instances of the same class that
this commit deliberately does NOT change, because for them deleting the
initializer would be a semantic change rather than a repair - both use a
negative sentinel over a domain where 0 is legitimate, so the correct remedy
is to make the member nullable:

  AtomicActionState.FailedStepIndex   (-1 = no fault; a saga faulting on step 0
                                       writes 0, which is omitted, and reloads
                                       as "no fault")
  LeafSnapshotBlob.SnapshotOffset     (-1 = nothing captured; a snapshot
                                       consistent through WAL offset 0 reloads
                                       as "nothing captured")

They are carried as documented exemptions, so the gate stays live for any new
instance while these are tracked separately.

Refs #1883

* fix: make sentinel-initialised persisted state members nullable

AtomicActionState.FailedStepIndex and LeafSnapshotBlob.SnapshotOffset
used a -1 initializer to mean "unset". A grain-storage serializer omits
any member equal to default(T), so a legitimately written 0 was dropped
from the blob and the initializer resurrected the sentinel on load.

A saga that faulted on its FIRST step wrote 0, had it omitted, and
reloaded reporting no forward fault - feeding the compensation decision.
A leaf snapshot consistent through WAL offset 0 reloaded claiming
nothing had been captured, discarding the blob on exactly the
cold-restart path it exists to serve.

Unlike the two bool members fixed for issue 1886, the initializer could
not simply be removed: 0 is a legitimate value here rather than an off
state, so removing it would make "unset" indistinguishable from a real
zero - a semantic change, not a repair. Both members become nullable
instead, so absent means null means unset and a written 0 is no longer a
default the serializer may drop.

The [Id(n)] numbers are unchanged. The public AtomicActionOutcome
surface keeps int/-1 via a boundary projection, so there is no public
API change.

The two documented exemptions in the persisted-state contract test are
deleted; that gate is now exemption-free.

fix: stop the Dashboard stating disk and memory verdicts it never measured (#2043)

* fix: stop the Dashboard stating disk and memory verdicts it never measured

* fix: stop the Dashboard stating disk and memory verdicts it never measured

Two tiles asserted facts about the user's hardware that the app had not checked.

P1, disk. DiskHealthService swallows ManagementException,
UnauthorizedAccessException and COMException and returns its partially-filled list,
so a Storage WMI namespace that is broken or access-denied reaches HealthScoreService
as an EMPTY list rather than as an exception. ComputeDiskScore returned 100, and
ScanSmartHealthAsync branches on >= 90 to set "All SMART indicators healthy" in
green. A machine whose disk health could not be read at all was told its disks were
fine.

The same shape applied to ComputeRamScore and ComputeUptimeScore, which returned 100
for a null snapshot, while BuildRecommendations suppressed everything because each arm
requires a non-null source — so a machine where all three reads failed reported a
perfect score with no advice and nothing anywhere saying why.

The file already argued the opposite principle twelve lines below the bug: "80, not
100, for a drive we know nothing about: absent evidence is not a clean bill of health,
and this is the only case that reaches it." That last clause was false. The empty-list
path is a stronger absence of evidence and was scored more generously.

P2, memory. The tile titled "No memory errors (30 days)" classified on RamScore, which
is derived entirely from memory USAGE percent — unrelated to hardware errors. The
service that answers this question exists, is a registered singleton, and its doc says
"Scans the System event log for hardware-error events (WHEA) in the last 30 days";
it was consumed only by SystemHealthViewModel, which words the same result correctly.
Both directions were wrong: real WHEA errors at 40% usage read as "No memory errors",
and a healthy machine at 85% usage read as "Memory issues detected" while System
Health said the opposite.

An unread component now scores UnknownComponentScore (80), the same value the
per-drive unknown rule already used, and HealthScoreResult carries
UnavailableComponents so a caller can say "could not be read" instead of reading a
verdict out of a fallback number — unknown is not "degrading" either. Both alert
decisions became pure internal statics, matching ClassifyAppUpdates in the same file;
previously both lived inside a Dispatcher.BeginInvoke callback where no test could
reach them.

Four existing tests required the defect, one per arm, and all four are rewritten to
pin the rule instead: ComputeDiskScore_NullDisks_Returns100,
ComputeDiskScore_EmptyList_Returns100, ComputeRamScore_NullSnapshot_Returns100 and
ComputeUptimeScore_NullSnapshot_Returns100. The battery arm never had the bug — it
redistributes its weight when there is no battery rather than scoring one — and the
remaining Returns100 tests all assert a MEASURED perfect result, which is correct and
untouched.

Red before, green after, under five mutations. Restoring the 100 turns the two disk
tests red; removing the unavailable branch turns the SMART test red; making WHEA
errors invisible turns two red; reporting a failed scan as green turns the
scan-failed test red; and raising UnknownComponentScore to 95 turns red the test that
owns that number.

That last mutation first exposed a flaw in my own tests: the arm tests asserted
Equal(UnknownComponentScore, ...), comparing the constant to itself, so raising it
moved both sides of the assertion and only one test noticed. The number now has a
dedicated test pinning the literal 80 and its relationship to the >= 90 green
threshold.

Scope: the audit's fuller suggestion — nullable component scores with the weights
redistributed over components that actually reported, as the battery arm already
does — is a better model but changes HealthScoreResult's shape, the CLI's JSON
contract and the gauge's inputs. Left as a separate change; this one makes missing
evidence representable and stops the false verdicts.

feat(ci): aim CodeRabbit at risk instead of standing it down (#3625)

* feat(ci): aim CodeRabbit at risk instead of standing it down

The stand-down was suspended yesterday because it forfeited the allowance rather
than moving it: 21 PRs skipped on a `clean` verdict whose total findings were
ZERO. This is what should have been there instead.

THE DIFFERENCE IS WHAT THE LABEL DEPENDS ON. `!claude-reviewed` skipped a PR
because the OTHER REVIEWER had an opinion about it, so the lane's recall decided
CodeRabbit's coverage -- and the lane's recall was zero. `!low-risk` skips a PR
because of what the DIFF IS: prose, a lockfile, generated output. No reviewer's
verdict can move that.

WHY AIM AT ALL. CodeRabbit's fair usage is keyed to a developer identity on a
rolling window, not to a repository, and it was rate-limited on 27 of a 40-PR
sample. Its reviews therefore land on whichever PRs arrive while the window has
room -- arrival order, which is noise. Aiming is the only lever that does not
require buying more.

THE ERROR DIRECTION IS CHOSEN, and it decides every rule. A misclassified
low-risk PR LOSES a review; a misclassified high-risk PR only wastes one. So a
PR is low-risk only when EVERY file is something nobody reads line by line, and
an unrecognised path, an unreadable file list, a changeset, a workflow file and
a test-only diff all count as needing review. There is no "probably fine".

TEST-ONLY DIFFS ARE HIGH RISK, which is the opposite of the usual call and
correct here: this repository's memory is a taxonomy of tests that cannot fail --
oracles sharing the defect under test, expected values derived from the code
under test, ratio assertions trivially true at zero. A test-only diff is exactly
where a second reader pays.

A BUG ITS OWN TEST CAUGHT, before it shipped. `.changeset/nice-cats.md` matched
the `\.md$` prose rule and classified as low-risk -- the one class the docblock
singles out as dangerous, because a changeset naming a package that does not
exist fails the RELEASE workflow, which only runs on main. That is #3175: twelve
wrong version bumps. A narrow rule stated in prose and a broad pattern in code is
the shape this repository keeps paying for; `NEVER_LOW_RISK` makes the prose
executable, and deleting it turns the suite red.

`pull_request_target`, so the classifier runs from the BASE branch: a PR must not
be able to edit the rule that decides whether it gets a second reviewer. Nothing
checks out or executes PR code -- the only input is the file LIST, read from the
API, and `--paginate` because a truncated list reads as "fewer risky files",
which is the losing direction.

The label is CLEARED as well as applied, or a PR that grows a real file after its
first push would keep the first commit's verdict and silence CodeRabbit for the
rest of its life. And the step reads the label back and says which way it went,
because it is best-effort by necessity and the last best-effort label step spent
a whole day silently never being applied behind three green checks.

8 classifier tests, 144 across the lane, five repo gates.

* fix(ci): low-risk must mean the LANE reads it, or the PR is reviewed by nobody

Pre-flight review caught a regression before it shipped, and it is the exact
shape this system exists to refuse.

The classifier borrowed the lane's own `isExcluded` with an OR. But that
predicate answers a DIFFERENT question -- "is it worth spending model tokens on
this" -- and it covers `fixtures/`, `pkg/`, `dist/`, `.snap` and lockfiles, all
of which the LANE ALSO SKIPS: `claude-review.yml` turns them into NO_FILES and
never runs the model.

So a fixtures-only or `Cargo.lock`-only PR would have had CodeRabbit labelled
OFF and no Claude review either. Reviewed by nobody -- while the workflow's
read-back printed "✅ the Claude lane still reviews it", which is false. Absence
reading as success, in the step added specifically to prevent that. PR #3558 is
a live instance of the lockfile shape, and `packages/viewer/src/fixtures/` of
the other.

The two predicates are ANDed now: a path is low-risk only when it is prose AND
the lane will actually read it. Anything the lane skips is high-risk by
construction, because there CodeRabbit is the only reader left. That also
restores the module's own stated rule -- losing a review is worse than wasting
one -- which the borrowed OR had quietly inverted for a whole class of paths.

The echo says what is true now, and a test pins seven such paths as reviewable.
Putting the OR back turns the suite red.

9 classifier tests, five repo gates.

Entry angle: four variants tested, all reverted, and the sweep that
suggested them was measuring geometry the game cannot produce

The rival's launch is `playerAngle + PI` — it always mirrors to the far
side, so every round in the game opens with the same geometry and the
player's own entry angle (which is `Math.random()`) is inert. That looked
like the same bug class as the spin policy, where the AI answering the
player made the player's choice worthless.

FORCING THE OFFSET AND SWEEPING IT SEEMED TO CONFIRM IT:

    offset    hits/round   adjacency   round
       0deg      6.75        35.9%     10.68s
      90deg      5.59        27.6%     10.69s
     180deg      5.42        27.4%      9.06s

Read straight, the game is pinned to its least eventful configuration and
is losing a quarter of its contact to do it.

THAT SWEEP IS WRONG, and the reason is the useful part. It forces both
entry ANGLES while leaving each side's chosen entry DEPTH alone — and the
two are coupled, since stamina enters deep at 0.35 and everything else
shallow at 0.05. It therefore measures launch geometry the game never
actually creates. Same family as the two instrument failures already
recorded this session: a lever not connected to the thing measured, and a
rate taken against a denominator nobody plays.

RE-MEASURED ON THE REAL PATH, each side choosing its own launch and only
this one formula changing:

    mirror (shipped)     round  9.91s   hits 6.19   adjacency 33.9%
    archetype, mid       round 11.46s   hits 5.61   adjacency 28.9%
    archetype, closer    round 10.35s   hits 5.99   adjacency 34.1%
    archetype, closest   round 11.71s   hits 6.45   adjacency 32.1%

The closest variant lands the most hits — over an 18% longer round. Per
second that is 0.551 against the mirror's 0.625. Every variant spreads
the same action more thinly, so the value that was already there wins.

WHAT THE SWEEP DID ESTABLISH, and it is worth keeping: the offset is not
a win-rate lever at all. First-launcher win rate runs 46.8% to 54.4%
across the full range, noise at n=79. It moves the texture of a round and
not who takes it — so anyone retuning it later is trading pacing against
pacing and nothing else, and should not expect balance to move.

That also settles whether the player should get to aim their launch: not
worth a control. Spin direction was worth 24 points and was hidden; this
is worth none and is better left alone.

Reverted to the original line, with the measurements kept above it so the
next person does not repeat the sweep.

218 tests, build verified by exit code.

Two portals, one origin, one set of session keys

The technical-admin console and the employee portal are separate sign-ins
served from the same origin, and both wrote their session to
hrp.accessToken / hrp.refreshToken. Signing into either one overwrote the
other. localStorage is shared across every tab of an origin, so this was never
confined to a single window: opening the console signed you out of the
employee portal in the tab next door, and the abandoned tab started failing on
its next request with no explanation.

Each portal now keeps its session under its own keys, chosen from the path at
the moment the key is read rather than once at module load -- these are asked
for after navigation, and a value captured at import time would name whichever
portal the tab first opened on. Signing out of one no longer signs you out of
the other, because clear() only removes that portal's pair.

Nothing else reads the raw keys, and the 401 handler already branched on the
same path check, so its behaviour is unchanged.

38 web tests, typecheck and build clean. The new test was verified by
restoring the shared key and watching both cases fail.

league_simulation.project_team_roster picked each team's rotation_size

most recent season was short due to injury (Dereck Lively II: 7 GP at

weighted by recency and by games played.

two years ago) got inflated toward his old role and wrongly displaced
